position: mid — before the main verb, after *be* and the first auxiliary; also alone as an answer
contrast: *Surely* is not a synonym: *Certainly he knows* states a fact, but *Surely you know him* means “I'd be amazed if you didn't” and asks for agreement. As a reply, *Certainly* is polite and a little formal; everyday American speech says *Sure*.

senses.gloss: Without any doubt; definitely.
examples: She *certainly* knows how to throw a party.
It's *certainly* not the cheapest option, but it's the best.
Things will *certainly* get busier after the holidays.

senses.gloss: Used as a polite answer to agree or give permission: yes, of course; *certainly not* is a firm no.
examples: “Could you help me with this box?” “*Certainly*.”
“Can I pay by card?” “*Certainly* — right over here.”
“May I borrow your car tonight?” “*Certainly* not.”

position: mid — before the main verb, after *be* and the first auxiliary; also alone as an answer
contrast: Order with *not* changes the meaning: *It's definitely not true* = точно неправда, but *It's not definitely true* = не факт, что правда. Do not use it for Russian *определённый* = “certain, particular”: *в определённой степени* is *to a certain extent*, not *definitely to some degree*.

senses.gloss: Without any doubt; for sure.
examples: I'm *definitely* coming to your party.
That was *definitely* the best pizza I've ever had.
We *definitely* need more chairs for Saturday.

senses.gloss: Used as an answer to say a strong yes or no.
examples: “Are you going to vote?” “*Definitely*.”
“Would you go back to that hotel?” “*Definitely* not.”

senses.gloss: In a fixed, final way, so that there is no more doubt or change.
examples: Nothing has been *definitely* decided yet.
We can't say *definitely* when the store will reopen.

type: stance — what everyone should know; also manner
position: mid — before the main verb, after *be* and the first auxiliary; also front with a comma
contrast: False friend: Russian *очевидно* often means “probably, it seems” (*Очевидно, он опоздал на поезд*) — that is *apparently* or *evidently* in English. *Obviously* means “as anyone can see” and can sound rude if the listener did not know: *Obviously, the meeting is at three.*

senses.gloss: Used to say that something is clear or expected and should need no explanation.
examples: *Obviously*, we can't leave the kids home alone.
“Did you tell her?” “*Obviously* not.”
We'll *obviously* pay you back as soon as we can.

senses.gloss: In a way that is easy to see or notice.
examples: She was *obviously* upset about something.
He'd *obviously* never cooked a turkey before.
The dog was *obviously* hungry.

position: mid — before the main verb, after *be* and the first auxiliary; also front with a comma
contrast: *Evidently* is closer to Russian *очевидно, по-видимому* (a conclusion) than *obviously* is. It is a little more formal than *apparently*, and like *apparently* it can also pass on what the speaker has heard: *Evidently, she quit last week* = судя по всему (говорят), она уволилась.

senses.gloss: Based on what you can see or have found out; apparently.
examples: The owners had *evidently* left in a hurry.
*Evidently*, nobody told him about the schedule change.
“Did the package come?” “*Evidently* not.”

senses.gloss: In a way that is plain to see; clearly.
examples: He was *evidently* nervous — his hands were shaking.
She was *evidently* pleased with the results.

type: stance — what the speaker has heard or what seems true
position: mid — before the main verb, after *be* and the first auxiliary; also front with a comma, and end in speech
contrast: False friend: *apparently* does not mean *явно, очевидно*. The adjective can (*for no apparent reason* = без видимой причины), but the adverb almost always means “I heard” or “it seems”: *Apparently he's rich* = говорят, он богат.

senses.gloss: According to what you have heard or read, though you cannot be sure.
examples: *Apparently*, the restaurant is closing next month.
He's *apparently* moving to Denver.
The meeting got canceled, *apparently*.

senses.gloss: Seeming to be true from what you can see, though it may not be.
examples: The back door had *apparently* been forced open.
It started as an *apparently* harmless joke.

position: mid — before the main verb, after *be* and the first auxiliary; also front with a comma
contrast: *Presumably* is the speaker's own reasonable guess, which they expect to be right. Russian news style *предположительно* (*предположительно, преступник*) is *allegedly* or *suspected* in English, not *presumably*.

senses.gloss: Used to say that you think something is very likely true, based on what you know.
examples: You're *presumably* tired after such a long flight.
*Presumably*, the package will arrive tomorrow.
He left early, *presumably* to beat the traffic.

position: mid — before the main verb, after *be* and the first auxiliary, and before a negative auxiliary (*probably won't*)
contrast: Position with a negative: *He probably won't come*, not *He won't probably come*. Russian *наверное* is often a polite hedge; *probably* really means “more likely than not”, so *I'll probably come* is a weak promise.

senses.gloss: Very likely; more likely than not.
examples: It'll *probably* rain this afternoon.
She *probably* won't remember me.
“Are you coming tonight?” “*Probably*.”

position: mid — before the main verb, after the modal (*can't possibly*); also alone as an answer
contrast: *Can't possibly* is not “maybe can't” — it means “there is no way”: *I can't possibly finish by Friday* = я никак не успею к пятнице. In a request, *Could you possibly…?* is extra polite, not doubtful.

senses.gloss: Perhaps; used when something could be true but is not certain.
examples: The drive could take three hours, *possibly* more.
It was *possibly* the worst movie I've ever seen.
“Will you finish today?” “*Possibly*.”

senses.gloss: Used with *can* or *could* for emphasis: in any way at all.
examples: I can't *possibly* eat all that.
How could anyone *possibly* believe him?
We did everything we *possibly* could.

senses.gloss: Used to make a request more polite.
examples: Could you *possibly* turn the music down a little?
Could I *possibly* borrow your notes from Tuesday?

position: front — usually at the start of the clause; also before a number, and alone as an answer
contrast: *Maybe* (one word) is the adverb; *may be* (two words) is a modal and a verb: *Maybe he is right* = *He may be right*. Never *He maybe right*. *Maybe* is informal; in writing *perhaps* is more common.

senses.gloss: Perhaps; possibly.
examples: *Maybe* she's stuck in traffic.
We could go to the beach, or *maybe* the lake.
“Are you coming with us?” “*Maybe*.”

senses.gloss: Used to make a suggestion politely.
examples: *Maybe* we should call a plumber.
*Maybe* you could ask your dad for help.

senses.gloss: Used before a number: about, approximately.
examples: There were *maybe* fifty people at the meeting.
It's *maybe* a ten-minute walk from here.

position: front — at the start of the clause; also mid, especially before an adjective or noun phrase
contrast: *Perhaps* is more formal than *maybe*; in everyday American conversation *maybe* is far more common. Unlike *maybe*, *perhaps* sits easily in mid position: *It was perhaps her best book*.

senses.gloss: Possibly; maybe.
examples: *Perhaps* the letter got lost in the mail.
It was *perhaps* the most important decision of her career.
“Will he agree?” “*Perhaps*.”

senses.gloss: Used to make a suggestion, offer or request more polite.
examples: *Perhaps* you'd like to wait in the lobby.
*Perhaps* we could discuss this after lunch?

senses.gloss: Used before a number: about, approximately.
examples: *Perhaps* two hundred people showed up.
The house is *perhaps* a mile from the highway.

position: mid — before the main verb, after *be* and the first auxiliary; also front with a comma
form: un- + *doubted* + -ly; the *b* is silent and the -ed is a full syllable
contrast: *Undoubtedly* means full certainty; *doubtless*, despite its look, often means only “probably”.

senses.gloss: Without any doubt; certainly.
examples: She is *undoubtedly* the best player on the team.
Prices will *undoubtedly* go up again next year.
*Undoubtedly*, the new law will be challenged in court.

type: stance — a claim the speaker supports
position: mid — usually right before the adjective or noun phrase it comments on; also front with a comma
contrast: False friend: the adjective *arguable* often means “спорный”, but *arguably* supports the claim — *He is arguably the best* = пожалуй, он лучший (and the speaker thinks so). It is not doubt and not *доказуемо*.

senses.gloss: Used to say that something can reasonably be claimed, and the speaker believes it, though others may disagree.
examples: He is *arguably* the greatest basketball player of all time.
It was *arguably* the most important invention of the century.
*Arguably*, the city's best food is found in its smallest restaurants.

type: stance — a claim that has not been proved
position: mid — before the main verb, after *be* and the first auxiliary
form: -ly from *alleged*; the -ed is a full syllable
contrast: In news reports *allegedly* protects the writer: someone has made the claim, usually an accusation, but it is not proved. It is not the speaker's own guess — that is *presumably*.

senses.gloss: According to what someone has said, especially in an accusation that has not been proved.
examples: The suspect *allegedly* stole more than $10,000 from his employer.
He was *allegedly* driving over 90 miles an hour.
The company *allegedly* hid the test results from regulators.

type: stance — what people say, with doubt
position: mid — before the main verb, after *be* and the first auxiliary; also front with a comma
form: -ly from *supposed*; the -ed is a full syllable: /zɪd/
contrast: *Supposedly* signals that the speaker doubts the claim (якобы), unlike *presumably* (the speaker believes it). The form *supposably* is heard but counts as an error.

senses.gloss: According to what people say or believe, though the speaker doubts it is true.
examples: The old house is *supposedly* haunted.
This cream *supposedly* makes you look ten years younger.
He was *supposedly* sick, but I saw him at the game.

position: mid — before the main verb, after *be* and the first auxiliary; also front with a comma
form: -ly from *reported*; the -ed is a full syllable
contrast: *Reportedly* only says the news comes from reports and is not confirmed; *allegedly* says someone has been accused of something.

senses.gloss: According to what has been reported, though it is not confirmed.
examples: The singer is *reportedly* planning a world tour.
*Reportedly*, the two companies have been in talks for months.
The storm *reportedly* left thousands without power.

position: before its word — usually before an adjective; also front with a comma, or mid
contrast: Before an adjective, *seemingly* hints that the look is false: *a seemingly simple question* = казалось бы, простой вопрос. At the front it is closer to *apparently*: *Seemingly, nobody noticed* = судя по всему, никто не заметил.

senses.gloss: Appearing to be something, especially when this may not be true.
examples: It was a *seemingly* simple question, but nobody could answer it.
We waited in a *seemingly* endless line of cars.
The *seemingly* quiet town had a lot of secrets.

senses.gloss: As far as anyone can tell; apparently.
examples: *Seemingly*, nobody noticed the mistake.
The two men were *seemingly* unaware of each other.

type: stance — the speaker's feeling about it
position: front — with a comma; also mid, or end after a comma

senses.gloss: Used to say that something good happened, or something bad was avoided, by good luck.
examples: *Fortunately*, no one was hurt in the accident.
We *fortunately* had an umbrella in the car.
*Fortunately* for us, the store was still open.

type: stance — the speaker's feeling about it
position: front — with a comma; also mid, or end after a comma
contrast: *Unfortunately* is the everyday English for *к сожалению* — in emails, refusals and bad news. *Regrettably* is formal and official, *sadly* adds real emotion, and *to my regret* sounds stiff.

senses.gloss: Used to say that something is bad news or not what you wanted.
examples: *Unfortunately*, the concert is sold out.
I *unfortunately* won't be able to make it on Friday.
The package went to the wrong address, *unfortunately*.

type: stance — the speaker's feeling about it
position: front — with a comma; also mid

senses.gloss: Used to say that something good happened because of good luck.
examples: *Luckily*, I had my phone with me.
We *luckily* found a parking spot right outside.
*Luckily* for him, the police officer let him go with a warning.

type: stance — the speaker's feeling about it; also manner and degree
position: front — with a comma as a stance adverb; end or mid in the manner sense; before its word in the degree sense
comparison: more/most — in the manner sense only (*more sadly*); not gradable as a stance adverb
modifies: clauses, verbs, adjectives and participles (*sadly mistaken*)
contrast: Position changes the meaning: *Sadly, she left* = к сожалению, она ушла; *She left sadly* = она ушла грустная. *Sadly mistaken* is degree: “very wrong”, with no sadness at all.

senses.gloss: Used to say that something is sad or regrettable; unfortunately.
examples: *Sadly*, the old theater was torn down in 2015.
Her grandfather *sadly* passed away last spring.
*Sadly*, the museum is closed on Mondays.

senses.gloss: In a sad way.
examples: She smiled *sadly* and waved goodbye.
He shook his head *sadly*.

senses.gloss: Very much or completely, in a bad way — before a few adjectives and participles.
examples: If you think I'll pay for that, you're *sadly* mistaken.
The old park has been *sadly* neglected.

type: stance — the speaker's feeling about it; also degree
position: front — with a comma; mid; before its word in the degree sense
contrast: *Regrettably* means “it is a pity”; *regretfully* means “with regret, feeling sorry” (*She regretfully declined*). Many Americans use *regretfully* for both, but careful writing keeps them apart. *Regrettably* is formal — in conversation say *unfortunately*.

senses.gloss: Used in formal speech or writing to say that something is unfortunate.
examples: *Regrettably*, we are unable to offer you a position at this time.
The event has *regrettably* been canceled.

senses.gloss: To a degree that is a pity — before an adjective or quantifier.
examples: *Regrettably* few students signed up for the program.
The city's response to the flooding was *regrettably* slow.

position: before its word — before an adjective or adverb; front with a comma as a stance adverb
comparison: more/most — *even more amazingly*, at the front
contrast: Position changes the meaning: *Amazingly, she sang well* = удивительно, что она хорошо спела; *She sang amazingly well* = она пела потрясающе.

senses.gloss: To a very great or surprising degree; extremely.
examples: The food was *amazingly* good.
She handled the bad news *amazingly* well.
The tickets were *amazingly* cheap.

senses.gloss: Used to say that something is very surprising.
examples: *Amazingly*, nobody was hurt in the crash.
The old car *amazingly* still runs.
Even *more amazingly*, the dog found its way home.

position: before its word — before an adjective or adverb; front with a comma as a stance adverb
comparison: more/most — *even more surprisingly*, *most surprisingly*, at the front
contrast: False friend: Russian *неожиданно* often means “suddenly” (*Неожиданно он встал*) — that is *suddenly*, not *surprisingly*. *Surprisingly* only says the fact was not expected. *Not surprisingly* at the front means “as expected”.

senses.gloss: To a degree that you would not expect.
examples: The test was *surprisingly* easy.
The hotel was *surprisingly* cheap for Manhattan.
He took the news *surprisingly* well.

senses.gloss: Used to say that a fact or event is not what you expected.
examples: *Surprisingly*, the youngest runner won the race.
*Not surprisingly*, the plan failed.
*Most surprisingly*, nobody complained about the price.

ru: к счастью, слава богу; с благодарностью
position: front — with a comma as a stance adverb; mid or end in the manner sense
contrast: Position changes the meaning: *Thankfully, he took the money* = слава богу, он взял деньги; *He took the money thankfully* = взял деньги с благодарностью. The stance use is standard American English.

senses.gloss: Used to say you are glad and relieved that something happened or did not happen.
examples: *Thankfully*, the rain stopped before the wedding.
The surgery was *thankfully* a success.
*Thankfully*, nobody was home when the tree fell.

senses.gloss: In a grateful way.
examples: He smiled *thankfully* at the nurse.
She sank *thankfully* into the hot bath.

type: stance — an unexpected reversal; also manner
position: front — with a comma as a stance adverb; end in the manner sense
comparison: more/most — *even more ironically*, *most ironically*, at the front; *more ironically* in the manner sense
contrast: Strictly, *ironically* needs a result opposite to what you would expect (*по иронии судьбы*); Americans often use it loosely for any coincidence or bad luck, which careful writers dislike.

senses.gloss: Used to say that something happened in the opposite way to what you would expect, in a strange or funny way.
examples: *Ironically*, the fire station burned down.
The anti-smoking ad was, *ironically*, paid for by a tobacco company.
*Ironically*, the more he tried to relax, the more stressed he got.

senses.gloss: In an ironic way, meaning the opposite of what you say.
examples: “Great job,” he said *ironically*, looking at the broken vase.
She smiled *ironically* when he called it a small problem.

position: front — with a comma as a stance adverb; mid before a verb or adjective (*predictably dull*); end in the manner sense
comparison: more/most — in the manner sense (*more predictably*); not gradable as a stance adverb
contrast: Position changes the meaning: *Predictably, he lost* = как и следовало ожидать, он проиграл; *He played predictably* = он играл предсказуемо.

senses.gloss: Used to say that something happened exactly as people expected.
examples: *Predictably*, the kids got bored after ten minutes.
Gas prices, *predictably*, went up before the holiday weekend.
The proposal was *predictably* rejected by the board.

senses.gloss: In a way that can be predicted, often too easily.
examples: The movie ended *predictably*, with a big wedding.
The new software behaves *more predictably* than the old version.

type: stance — something odd; also manner and degree
position: end — in the manner sense; front with a comma as a stance adverb; before its word before an adjective
comparison: more/most — in the manner sense (*more curiously*); not gradable as a stance adverb
contrast: Position changes the meaning: *She asked about him curiously* = спросила с любопытством; *Curiously, she asked about him* = странно, что она спросила. It is not *курьёзно* (funny, absurd).

senses.gloss: In a way that shows you want to know about something.
examples: The cat watched the puppy *curiously*.
She looked at me *curiously*, as if trying to remember my name.

senses.gloss: Used to say that a fact is strange or hard to explain.
examples: *Curiously*, nobody heard the alarm.
*Curiously* enough, the letter had no return address.

senses.gloss: Strangely, in a way that is hard to explain — before an adjective.
examples: The street was *curiously* empty for a Saturday night.
He seemed *curiously* calm after the accident.

ru: что вполне понятно, по понятным причинам
position: mid — before the adjective or main verb, after *be*; also front with a comma
contrast: *Understandably* does not mean “in a way that is easy to understand” (*понятно объяснить* = *explain clearly*). It means “and it is easy to see why”: *She was understandably upset* = она расстроилась, что вполне понятно.

senses.gloss: Used to say that a feeling or reaction is natural and easy to understand.
senses.ru: что вполне понятно, по понятным причинам
examples: She was *understandably* upset about losing her job.
*Understandably*, many parents are worried about the new policy.
He's *understandably* nervous before the surgery.

type: stance — the speaker's hope; also manner
position: front — with a comma as a stance adverb; also mid; end in the manner sense
comparison: more/most — in the manner sense (*more hopefully*); not gradable as a stance adverb
contrast: Russian speakers tend to say *I hope* every time; *Hopefully* is the natural spoken choice and fully standard in American English. Position changes the meaning: *Hopefully, he'll call* = надеюсь, он позвонит; *He looked at the phone hopefully* = он с надеждой смотрел на телефон.

senses.gloss: Used to say what you hope will happen.
examples: *Hopefully*, we'll be home before dark.
The package should *hopefully* arrive by Friday.
“Will it be fixed soon?” “*Hopefully*.”

senses.gloss: In a hopeful way.
examples: The dog looked up at me *hopefully*.
She glanced *hopefully* at her phone.

position: front — with a comma; also mid after a comma
contrast: *Interestingly* introduces a fact; it is not a reply like *Интересно!* (say *Interesting!* or *That's interesting*), and it never means “I wonder”: *Интересно, придёт ли он* = *I wonder if he'll come*.

senses.gloss: Used to introduce a fact that the speaker finds interesting or unexpected.
examples: *Interestingly*, the town has more dogs than people.
*Interestingly* enough, she never learned to drive.
The study, *interestingly*, found no link between the two.

position: front — with a comma as a stance adverb; mid; end in the manner sense
comparison: more/most — in the manner sense (*more naturally*); not gradable as a stance adverb
contrast: Position changes the meaning: *Naturally, she smiled* = конечно, она улыбнулась; *She smiled naturally* = она улыбнулась непринуждённо. In *Just act natural*, Americans use the adjective, not *naturally*.

senses.gloss: Used to say that something is expected or normal; of course.
examples: *Naturally*, we want the best for our kids.
He was *naturally* disappointed with the result.
“Are you coming to the wedding?” “*Naturally*.”

senses.gloss: Because of the qualities someone or something is born with.
examples: Her hair is *naturally* curly.
Some people are just *naturally* good at math.
Public speaking doesn't come *naturally* to me.

senses.gloss: By nature, without chemicals, medicine or other outside help.
examples: The cut will heal *naturally* in a few days.
Radon is a *naturally* occurring gas.

senses.gloss: In a relaxed, normal way that is not forced.
examples: Try to smile *naturally* for the camera.
After a year in Chicago, she speaks English *more naturally*.

type: stance — how it is being said; also manner
position: front — with a comma as a stance adverb; also mid after a comma; end in the manner sense
comparison: more/most — in the manner sense (*more frankly*); not gradable as a stance adverb
contrast: *Frankly* usually warns that a blunt or critical opinion is coming, so it is sharper than *откровенно говоря*. *Frankly speaking* is understood but sounds non-native in American English — say *Frankly* or *To be honest*.

senses.gloss: Used to show that you are giving your honest opinion, even if it is not welcome.
examples: *Frankly*, I don't care what he thinks.
The service was, *frankly*, terrible.
*Quite frankly*, the plan is a disaster.

senses.gloss: In an open and honest way.
examples: She spoke *frankly* about her struggle with depression.
Can I talk to you *frankly* for a minute?

type: stance — how it is being said; also manner
position: front — with a comma as a stance adverb; mid before a verb (*I honestly thought*); end in the manner sense
comparison: more/most — in the manner sense (*more honestly*); not gradable as a stance adverb
contrast: Position changes the meaning: *Honestly, I don't know* comments on what you are saying (честно говоря, не знаю); *Answer the questions honestly* describes how (отвечайте честно). At the front with an annoyed tone, *Honestly!* means “ну честное слово!”.

senses.gloss: Used to stress that you are telling the truth or giving your real opinion.
examples: *Honestly*, I don't remember what I said.
I *honestly* thought the store was open.
“Did you like the movie?” “*Honestly*? Not really.”

senses.gloss: In an honest way, without lying or cheating.
examples: He made his money *honestly*.
Please answer every question *honestly*.

senses.gloss: Used to show that you are annoyed or disapprove.
senses.ru: ну честное слово, ну правда же
examples: *Honestly*, can't you ever be on time?
Oh, *honestly* — who leaves the milk out all night?

type: stance — speaking in earnest; also manner and degree
position: end — in the manner sense (*take it seriously*); before its word in the degree sense; front with a comma as a stance adverb
modifies: verbs, adjectives and participles (*seriously injured*), clauses
contrast: *Seriously ill* or *seriously injured* means тяжело болен, тяжело ранен — nothing about attitude. In American speech *Seriously?* means “Are you kidding me?” (Да ладно?), often with annoyance.

senses.gloss: In a serious way, with careful thought and not as a joke.
examples: You need to take your health *more seriously*.
We're *seriously* thinking about moving to Texas.
Nobody took his threats *seriously*.

senses.gloss: Badly; to a dangerous degree.
examples: Two people were *seriously* injured in the crash.
Her father is *seriously* ill.

senses.gloss: Used to show you mean what you say, or, as a question, to ask whether someone really means it.
examples: *Seriously*, though, are you okay?
You spent $500 on sneakers? *Seriously*?

senses.gloss: Informal: very, really.
examples: That pizza was *seriously* good.
I'm *seriously* tired of this weather.

position: front — with a comma; also mid
form: -ly from *admitted*; the -ed is a full syllable
contrast: *Admittedly* concedes a weak point and is normally followed by *but*. It does not mean *по общему признанию* (widely recognized) — that is *by all accounts* or *widely*.

senses.gloss: Used to admit that something is true, usually before a point that goes against it.
examples: *Admittedly*, the hotel was expensive, but the view was worth it.
The movie was, *admittedly*, a bit too long.
It's *admittedly* not a perfect solution, but it will work for now.

ru: по сути, в основном; в общем; практически
type: stance — summing up or simplifying; also degree
position: mid — before the main verb or adjective, after *be*; front with a comma when summing up
contrast: Russian *в принципе* is often *in principle* (in theory), not *basically*: *In principle I agree, but…*. Used as a filler in every sentence, *basically* sounds sloppy, especially in writing.

senses.gloss: In the most important ways; fundamentally.
examples: The two phones are *basically* the same.
Her story is *basically* true, though she left out some details.
He's *basically* a nice guy.

senses.gloss: Used to sum something up in a simple way.
examples: *Basically*, we ran out of money.
So *basically*, you're telling me I'm fired?

senses.gloss: Almost completely; practically.
examples: I'm *basically* done — just a few emails left.
He *basically* lives at his girlfriend's apartment.

position: mid — before the main verb, after *be* and the first auxiliary; front with a comma when correcting
contrast: False friend: *actually* never means *актуально* (relevant, up to date — say *relevant* or *current*), and *actual* is not *актуальный*. *В настоящее время* is *currently*, not *actually*.

senses.gloss: In fact; really — often in contrast to what was expected or what seems true.
examples: The restaurant looks small, but it's *actually* pretty big inside.
What *actually* happened that night?
I *actually* enjoyed the movie more than the book.

senses.gloss: Used to correct someone or to disagree politely.
examples: “You're from Ohio, right?” “*Actually*, I'm from Indiana.”
*Actually*, that's not quite what I said.

senses.gloss: Used when you change your mind or add a new request.
examples: *Actually*, I'll have the salmon instead.
*Actually*, could you pick up some milk on the way home?

senses.gloss: Used to show that something is surprising.
examples: He *actually* apologized — I couldn't believe it.
The kids *actually* cleaned their rooms without being asked.

type: stance — exactness of the words; also degree
position: mid — before the main verb or the word it stresses; end in the translation sense
contrast: Informal *literally* for emphasis (*I literally died laughing*) is very common but annoys many listeners; in writing keep it for things that are really true. *Take something literally* = понимать буквально.

senses.gloss: In the real, exact sense of the words, not as an exaggeration.
examples: He *literally* lives next door to his boss.
There were *literally* thousands of people in the square.
Don't take everything he says so *literally*.

senses.gloss: Word for word, in a translation or explanation of a name.
examples: The name *literally* means “red river.”
You can't translate this idiom *literally*.

senses.gloss: Informal: used for emphasis, even when the words are not really true.
examples: I *literally* died laughing.
My phone is *literally* glued to my hand.

type: stance — confirming or strengthening; also linking and degree
position: mid — after *be* and the first auxiliary; after its word in *very … indeed*; front before a stronger point
form: in + deed, written as one word
contrast: *Indeed* is formal in American English; in conversation *really* or *yes* is more natural, and *very good indeed* sounds British. A surprised *Действительно?* is *Really?*, not *Indeed?*.

senses.gloss: Used to confirm or agree that something is true.
examples: The results were *indeed* impressive.
“Is this your car?” “It is *indeed*.”
We did *indeed* receive your letter.

senses.gloss: Used to add a stronger point to what was just said.
examples: The plan is risky; *indeed*, it may be impossible.
Many students, *indeed* most of them, passed the test.

senses.gloss: Used after *very* and an adjective or adverb for extra emphasis.
examples: Thank you very much *indeed*.
It was a very good meal *indeed*.

senses.gloss: Used to repeat a question and show that you also wonder about it, or find it odd.
senses.ru: и правда, вот и я думаю
examples: “Why would anyone do that?” “Why *indeed*?”
“Who's paying for all this?” “Who *indeed*.”

position: mid — before the main verb, after *be* and the first auxiliary; also front
form: -less, with no -ly (*doubtlessly* exists but is rarer)
contrast: Despite its look, *doubtless* often means only “probably”: *You have doubtless heard the news* = вы, наверное, уже слышали. For full certainty use *undoubtedly* or *without a doubt*. It is formal and mostly written.

senses.gloss: Very probably; the speaker is fairly sure.
examples: You have *doubtless* heard the news by now.
He will *doubtless* complain about the price.

senses.gloss: Without doubt; certainly.
examples: It was *doubtless* the right decision.
Her talent is *doubtless* real, but she needs more practice.

position: mid — before the main verb or adjective, after *be*; front with a comma when summing up
contrast: False friend: *essentially* is not *существенно* (considerably): *Prices rose significantly*, not *essentially*. It means “in essence”, and is a more formal *basically*.

senses.gloss: In the most basic and important way; fundamentally.
examples: The two plans are *essentially* the same.
She is *essentially* a shy person.
The rules have stayed *essentially* unchanged since 1990.

senses.gloss: In effect; almost completely.
examples: The work is *essentially* finished — we just need to paint.
*Essentially*, what he's saying is no.

type: stance — sincerity and emphasis; also degree
position: before its word — before an adjective; mid before a verb
contrast: *Truly* is more formal and emotional than *really*. *Yours truly* at the end of a letter is formal (искренне ваш); in speech *yours truly* is a fixed phrase that jokingly means “me” (ваш покорный слуга).

senses.gloss: Really; to a very great degree — before an adjective.
examples: It was a *truly* beautiful wedding.
The view from the top is *truly* amazing.

senses.gloss: Sincerely; with real feeling.
examples: I'm *truly* sorry for your loss.
She *truly* loves her job.

senses.gloss: In fact and completely, not just in name or appearance.
examples: Nobody *truly* understands how the brain works.
Is he *truly* happy, or just pretending?

position: before its word — before an adjective; mid before a verb
contrast: Pronunciation trap: the last syllable of *genuine* is /ɪn/, not /aɪn/ like *wine*, so *genuinely* is JEN-yoo-in-lee.

senses.gloss: With real feeling; sincerely.
examples: She *genuinely* cares about her students.
I was *genuinely* happy for him.
He seemed *genuinely* surprised by the party.

senses.gloss: Really, and not just seeming to be.
examples: This is a *genuinely* new approach to the problem.
Is the painting *genuinely* old, or is it a copy?

position: mid — before the main verb, after *be* and the first auxiliary; *most likely* also front
comparison: more/most — *more likely*, *most likely*; also *more than likely* and *very likely*
form: flat — the same form as the adjective *likely* (*a likely result*)
contrast: Word-class trap: in *He is likely to win*, *likely* is an adjective (with *to*); the adverb has no *to*: *He will likely win*. US/UK split: bare *He'll likely win* is normal American English, while British English prefers *He'll probably win* or *most likely*.

senses.gloss: Probably.
examples: She'll *likely* be late again.
*Most likely*, the flight will be delayed.
Prices will *more than likely* go up next year.
